meta.name: Pulmonary Embolism — Post-Surgical DVT with S1Q3T3 Strain Pattern

patient.name: Diane Castellano
patient.chiefComplaint: Sudden shortness of breath and sharp chest pain that worsens with breathing

history.hpi: Patient is post-operative day 5 from a left total knee arthroplasty, largely sedentary at home since discharge. While getting up from the couch to do her prescribed walking exercises, she suddenly became short of breath with sharp, pleuritic left-sided chest pain. She denies any preceding trauma or new activity beyond standing. She reports her left calf has felt "tight and sore" for the past two days, which she attributed to post-surgical swelling.
pastMedical: Left total knee arthroplasty 5 days ago
medications: Oxycodone 5 mg PO PRN post-surgical pain
Enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily (DVT prophylaxis, last dose yesterday morning)
history.lastOralIntake: Toast and coffee about 90 minutes prior to onset
history.events: Husband called 911 immediately when she became acutely short of breath and could not catch her breath while standing

scene.location: Single-family home, living room, patient seated upright on the couch, leaning forward
scene.bystanders: Husband present, called 911 immediately, reports she was fine minutes earlier
visualCues: Patient seated upright, leaning forward, visibly anxious and short of breath
Splinting left side of chest with each breath
Left knee surgical dressing intact, left calf visibly more swollen than right
Walker positioned nearby, unused since the episode began
Compression stocking on right leg only, not yet applied to left

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 52-year-old post-surgical female sitting upright, tachypneic and anxious, with sudden-onset pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, shallow due to pleuritic pain, symmetric chest rise
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid and regular
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities; left calf swollen, tender to palpation, warm compared to right
otherFindings: Pleuritic chest pain 7/10, sharp, worse with inspiration
Left calf swelling, tenderness, and warmth, present for two days
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I can't... catch my breath... it hurts to breathe in."

transitions.condition: Crew applies supplemental oxygen, places the patient on a cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry, and obtains a 12-lead ECG as part of a full shock/respiratory assessment.
Crew attributes the presentation to anxiety or post-surgical pain without placing a cardiac monitor, obtaining a 12-lead, or escalating oxygen delivery despite hypoxia.

phases.name: O2 given, 12-lead performed
phases.description: Crew places the patient on high-flow oxygen, establishes cardiac monitoring, and obtains a 12-lead ECG, recognizing sinus tachycardia with an S1Q3T3 pattern suggestive of right heart strain from obstructive shock.
phases.triggerCondition: After the primary assessment identifies risk factors for venous thromboembolism (recent orthopedic surgery, immobility, unilateral leg swelling) alongside sudden dyspnea and hypoxia, the crew escalates oxygen, applies monitoring, and obtains a 12-lead ECG showing the classic S1Q3T3 strain pattern.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic, improved comfort with high-flow O2, still splinting
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid and regular
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Strength intact in all extremities; left calf findings unchanged
otherFindings: 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3 pattern (deep S wave in lead I, Q wave and inverted T wave in lead III)
SpO2 improved from 89% to 93% on high-flow O2
No hepatomegaly or JVD on exam
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "That oxygen helps a little, but it still hurts to breathe deep."

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply supplemental O2 titrated to 94-98% saturation; attach cardiac monitor and pulse oximetry
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation. Cardiac monitor. Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion)
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxia and provides continuous monitoring for a patient with suspected obstructive shock.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain 12-lead ECG; recognize S1Q3T3 strain pattern consistent with obstructive shock from PE
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: EKG Determination of type of shock ... Obstructive (e.g., pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax)
expectedActions.rationale: Identifying the strain pattern alongside VTE risk factors (recent surgery, immobility, unilateral leg swelling) points directly at PE as the obstructive cause.

expectedActions.shortAction: Establish IV access; if unsuccessful within 2 attempts or 90 seconds, place IO
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Establish IV access. If unable to obtain within two attempts or less than 90 seconds, place an IO needle
expectedActions.rationale: Vascular access is needed in case of decompensation into overt obstructive shock.

transitions.condition: Oxygen, monitoring, and IV access are in place; crew provides advance hospital notification and transports promptly without over-aggressive fluid administration.

phases.name: Supportive care and transport initiated
phases.description: Patient remains hemodynamically stable on high-flow O2 with IV access established. Crew provides advance notification of suspected PE/obstructive shock and transports promptly, avoiding large-volume fluid boluses that could worsen right heart strain.
phases.triggerCondition: With oxygen, monitoring, and IV access established and the S1Q3T3 pattern recognized, the crew provides advance notification to the receiving hospital and transports without delay, monitoring closely for signs of progression to overt shock.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Tachypneic but improved comfort, still guarding with deep breaths
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid and regular
otherFindings: SpO2 stable at 94% on high-flow O2
Advance notification given to receiving facility for suspected PE
No further deterioration in blood pressure
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "I'm still scared, but I can breathe a bit easier now."

expectedActions.shortAction: Provide advance hospital notification for suspected PE with obstructive shock physiology
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Provide advanced notification to the hospital
expectedActions.rationale: Allows the receiving facility to prepare for rapid CT angiography and possible thrombolytic therapy.

expectedActions.shortAction: Avoid large-volume fluid boluses; reassess for signs of worsening right heart strain
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Recognition of cardiogenic shock - If the patient condition deteriorates after fluid administration, rales or hepatomegaly develop, then consider cardiogenic shock and withholding further fluid administration
expectedActions.rationale: Obstructive shock from PE can behave like cardiogenic shock; aggressive fluids can worsen right ventricular strain.

phases.name: Attributed to anxiety, no 12-lead
phases.description: The crew attributes the sudden dyspnea and chest pain to anxiety or post-surgical pain, without escalating oxygen delivery or obtaining a 12-lead ECG. The unrecognized obstructive process progresses, and the patient becomes progressively more hypoxic and tachycardic.
phases.triggerCondition: Without a 12-lead ECG or full shock workup, the VTE risk factors and strain pattern go unrecognized. Oxygen is not escalated despite an SpO2 in the high 80s, and the patient's condition worsens as the obstruction progresses.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Increasingly labored, more rapid and shallow
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present, rapid and thready
otherFindings: SpO2 dropped to 82% on room air, no oxygen applied
No 12-lead obtained, VTE risk factors not documented

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize worsening hypoxia and falling EtCO2 as poor perfusion; escalate O2, monitor, and IV access immediately
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Pulse oximetry and EtCO2 (reading of less than 25 mmHg may be sign of poor perfusion) Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation
expectedActions.rationale: A falling EtCO2 with worsening hypoxia signals progressing obstructive shock that requires immediate escalation of care.
